lessons.title: Key Facts of the Chapter
lessons.notes_html:
Important Facts

  • A person who feels weak even though medical tests are normal is suffering from an illness — the person's own feeling of being unwell.
  • Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.
  • Feeling lonely affects a person's social health, even when the body is fit and active.
  • Lack of clean water mostly affects physical health.
  • Influenza is a disease that spreads from person to person.
  • Non-communicable diseases cannot spread from person to person.
  • Tuberculosis is a communicable disease.
  • Non-communicable diseases are best controlled by a healthy lifestyle and early screening.
  • Primary healthcare in Punjab is provided by Basic Health Units (BHUs).
  • A teaching hospital is the most suitable institution for heart surgery.

mcqs.why: Unsafe water causes infections and illness in the body, so lack of clean water mostly affects physical health, which means a fit body free from disease.

mcqs.why: Basic Health Units (BHUs), together with Rural Health Centres, provide primary healthcare as the community's first contact, giving basic treatment, prevention and vaccination near homes.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Illness, Disease and Disorder

Illness is the person's own feeling of being unwell, for example feeling weak even though medical tests are normal. Disease is a condition that can be found and diagnosed objectively, for example diabetes shown by a blood-sugar test. Disorder is an abnormality of function or structure, for example an anxiety disorder, which disturbs normal mental functioning even without a single germ or injury.

The Three Dimensions of Health

Physical well-being means a fit body, free from disease, with energy for daily work. Mental well-being means balanced emotions, clear thinking and the ability to cope with stress. Social well-being means healthy relationships, a sense of belonging and support from family and community.

Communicable and Non-Communicable Diseases

Communicable diseases spread from person to person through germs, for example tuberculosis, dengue and hepatitis. Non-communicable diseases do not spread between people; they develop from lifestyle, genes or age over time, for example diabetes, heart disease and cancer, and are controlled mainly by a healthy lifestyle and early screening.

Functions of the Three Levels of Healthcare in Punjab

Primary care is the first contact: Basic Health Units (BHUs) and Rural Health Centres (RHCs) give basic treatment, prevention, vaccination and maternal care near people's homes. Secondary care is specialist hospital care at Tehsil Headquarters (THQ) and District Headquarters (DHQ) hospitals for patients referred from primary care. Tertiary care is advanced specialist care at teaching hospitals, including major surgery, for the most serious cases.

Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR)

Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is the number of infants who die before their first birthday, per 1,000 live births in a year. Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) is the number of mothers who die from pregnancy-related causes, per 100,000 live births. Both are key indicators of a population's health and of its healthcare quality.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
The Three Dimensions of Health and How They Are Interrelated

Physical well-being is bodily fitness and freedom from disease; mental well-being is emotional balance and the ability to handle stress and think clearly; social well-being is good relationships and community support. They are interrelated: a long physical illness can cause low mood and isolation, poor mental health can weaken the body and appetite, and loneliness or family stress can harm both mind and body. That is why the WHO definition treats health as all three together, not merely the absence of disease.

Classification of Non-Communicable Diseases

Non-communicable diseases can be classified as: cardiovascular diseases, such as heart disease, hypertension and stroke; metabolic diseases, such as diabetes; cancers, such as lung or breast cancer; and chronic respiratory diseases, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). They share risk factors like unhealthy diet, tobacco, alcohol, inactivity and obesity, and they are usually long-lasting, so prevention and early screening matter more than a single cure.

Structure of the Healthcare System in Punjab

Punjab's healthcare system has three levels. Primary care (BHUs and RHCs) is the community's first contact, giving basic treatment, immunization, maternal and child care and health education. Secondary care (THQ and DHQ hospitals) receives referred patients and provides specialist doctors, surgery and inpatient care at tehsil and district level. Tertiary care (teaching hospitals) provides highly specialized treatment, major surgery and medical training, and also handles the most complex referrals from the lower levels.

BHUs, RHCs and THQ Hospitals Compared

A BHU is the smallest rural unit, staffed for basic outpatient care, immunization and maternal care for nearby villages. An RHC is larger, serving a wider rural area with more staff, beds and basic inpatient and laboratory services. A THQ hospital is a tehsil-level hospital with specialist doctors, an operating theatre and inpatient wards, receiving referrals that BHUs and RHCs cannot manage. In short, size, staff, equipment and the seriousness of cases handled all rise from BHU to RHC to THQ.

Functions of DHQ Hospitals and Teaching Hospitals

A DHQ hospital is the main hospital of a district: it provides specialist care, surgery, emergency and inpatient services, and it supervises and receives referrals from THQ hospitals, RHCs and BHUs in the district. A teaching hospital is attached to a medical college: besides advanced specialist care and major surgery (for example heart surgery), it trains doctors, nurses and allied health students and carries out medical research, so it handles the most complex cases in the province.

lessons.title: Group Activities — Model Guides
lessons.notes_html:
Write a short essay on the importance of primary healthcare in Punjab.

Model essay: Primary healthcare matters most in Punjab because it reaches people where they live. BHUs and RHCs treat common illnesses early, vaccinate children, care for mothers, and teach hygiene, so small problems do not become serious hospital cases. It is also the cheapest level of care, which protects poor families from heavy medical costs. A strong primary system therefore improves health indicators like infant and maternal mortality, reduces pressure on DHQ and teaching hospitals, and keeps communities healthier overall.

Create a poster on the prevention and management of hepatitis in Punjab.

Title: Protect Yourself from Hepatitis. Points: wash hands and drink clean water; get vaccinated against hepatitis; never share razors, needles or toothbrushes; ensure blood is screened before transfusion; eat hygienically prepared food. Management line: if you feel tired, lose appetite or notice yellow eyes/skin, visit a BHU or doctor at once and follow the prescribed treatment fully; do not self-medicate.

Write the challenges of managing cardiovascular diseases in Punjab.

The main challenges are late diagnosis, because many people ignore high blood pressure or chest discomfort until a crisis; lifestyle risks, including salty and fatty diets, tobacco, inactivity and obesity; limited access to specialist cardiac care in rural areas; the high cost of long-term medicines and procedures; and low awareness of warning signs and of the need for regular blood-pressure and sugar checks.

Create a presentation on improving immunization coverage in Punjab.

Model presentation guide: Slides: (1) Why immunization matters: it prevents deadly childhood diseases. (2) Current gaps: missed children in remote areas, myths, and lost vaccination cards. (3) Solutions: door-to-door campaigns, school and mosque announcements, lady health workers' follow-up visits, and record cards kept safely. (4) Call to action: every child fully vaccinated on schedule, with parents reminded of the next due date.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Peptic Ulcer and GERD

A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine (duodenum), caused mainly by stomach acid, infection with Helicobacter pylori, or overuse of painkillers like NSAIDs. GERD (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease) is the repeated flowing back of stomach acid into the oesophagus, causing heartburn and irritation of its lining.

Function of the Villi in the Small Intestine

Villi are tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine. They hugely increase its inner surface area, so digested nutrients can be absorbed efficiently into the blood. Each villus also contains tiny blood vessels that carry the absorbed nutrients away to the body.

Transmission of Typhoid Fever

Typhoid fever is transmitted by the faecal-oral route: the bacterium Salmonella Typhi spreads through food or water contaminated with the faeces of an infected person or carrier. Poor handwashing, unsafe water and unhygienic food handling are the usual routes.

Common Symptoms of Peptic Ulcers

The common symptoms are a burning or gnawing pain in the upper abdomen, especially when hungry or at night, bloating, nausea or vomiting, loss of appetite, and feeling full quickly. Severe cases may show vomiting of blood or black stools, which need urgent medical care.

Preventive Measures for Cholera

Drink only purified, boiled or bottled water; wash hands thoroughly with soap before eating and after using the toilet; store food properly in a refrigerator and avoid undercooked food; eat a balanced diet and stay hydrated; and use vaccination against cholera where it is offered. These are the chapter's own preventive measures for GI infections.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Functions of the Major Organs of the GI System

The mouth chews food and starts starch digestion with saliva. The oesophagus carries food to the stomach, which churns it and digests proteins with acid and enzymes. The small intestine completes digestion and absorbs nutrients through its villi. The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and stores waste. The liver makes bile, which helps digest fats; the gallbladder stores it; the pancreas supplies digestive enzymes and insulin; and the rectum and anus expel waste.

GERD and Peptic Ulcer: Causes, Symptoms and Treatments

GERD is caused by a weak valve between oesophagus and stomach, large meals before bed, obesity, spicy or fatty food and smoking; its symptoms are heartburn, acid taste, chest discomfort and cough; treatment is smaller meals, avoiding triggers, not lying down after eating, and acid-reducing medicines. Peptic ulcer is caused mainly by H. pylori infection, NSAID overuse and excess acid; symptoms are burning upper-abdominal pain, bloating and nausea; treatment is antibiotics for H. pylori, acid-reducing medicines, avoiding NSAIDs and alcohol, and medical follow-up.

Cholera, Typhoid Fever and Gastroenteritis

Cholera: pathogen Vibrio cholerae; transmission through contaminated water/food; symptoms are sudden watery diarrhoea, vomiting and dehydration; complications are severe dehydration, shock and death if untreated. Typhoid: pathogen Salmonella Typhi; faecal-oral transmission through contaminated food/water; symptoms are prolonged fever, headache, abdominal pain and weakness; complications include intestinal bleeding or perforation. Gastroenteritis: pathogens include viruses, bacteria and parasites; transmission through contaminated food, water or contact; symptoms are diarrhoea, vomiting, cramps and fever; complications are dehydration, especially dangerous in children.

Role of Diagnostic Tools in Diagnosing GI Disorders

Blood tests: a Complete Blood Count (CBC) can show infection (raised white cells), and Liver Function Tests (LFTs) measure enzymes and proteins to assess the liver and detect hepatitis. Imaging: X-rays outline the stomach or intestines, CT scans give detailed abdominal images for tumours, inflammation or blockages, MRI gives detailed soft-tissue images, and ultrasound examines the liver, gallbladder and pancreas. Endoscopy uses a flexible tube with a camera (endoscope) to look directly inside the GI tract and diagnose its disorders.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Gas Exchange in the Alveoli

Alveoli are tiny air sacs with very thin walls wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen from inhaled air diffuses across the alveolar wall into the blood, while carbon dioxide from the blood diffuses into the alveoli to be breathed out. This exchange works because gases move from higher to lower concentration across the thin membrane.

Asthma: Symptoms and Causes

Asthma symptoms are wheezing, coughing (often at night), shortness of breath and a feeling of tightness in the chest. It is caused by inflamed, sensitive airways that narrow in response to triggers such as dust, pollen, smoke, cold air, exercise or respiratory infections.

Significance of Vaccination in Preventing Respiratory Infections

Vaccination trains the immune system to recognize the virus, so infection is less likely and, if it happens, illness is usually milder with fewer complications and hospitalizations. The chapter notes the flu vaccine reduces severe illness, and COVID-19 vaccination, masks and distancing together reduce spread. Vaccination also protects vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated.

COPD: Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation

In COPD the airways and alveoli are progressively damaged, usually by long-term smoking or air pollution, so airflow is limited and the lungs cannot empty properly. Its clinical presentation is chronic cough with sputum, increasing breathlessness on exertion, wheezing and frequent chest infections, worsening slowly over years.

Diagnostic Methods Used to Evaluate Lung Function

Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs, including spirometry) measure how much air can be breathed in and out and how well the lungs work; chest X-ray and CT/MRI imaging show lung structure; pulse oximetry measures blood oxygen; sputum and blood tests detect infection; and a stethoscope examination identifies abnormal breathing sounds like wheezing or crackling.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Function of the Respiratory System

The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide: air enters through nose and mouth, passes the pharynx, trachea and bronchi into the lungs, and gas exchange occurs in the alveoli. It also warms, moistens and filters inhaled air, supports speech through the voice box, and helps regulate blood acidity by controlling carbon dioxide levels. The diaphragm and chest muscles drive breathing by expanding and contracting the lungs.

TB, Influenza and COVID-19: Transmission, Symptoms, Prevention and Treatment

TB: caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread through airborne droplets from coughing; symptoms are persistent cough over three weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss; prevention is BCG vaccination, ventilation and masks; treatment is a long course of anti-TB medicines taken completely. Influenza: spread by respiratory droplets; symptoms are fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and fatigue; prevention is flu vaccination and hygiene; treatment is rest, fluids and medicines for symptoms. COVID-19: spread by droplets, contaminated surfaces and direct contact; symptoms are fever, cough, loss of taste/smell and breathlessness; prevention is vaccination, masks and distancing; treatment is supportive care, with hospital care and oxygen for severe cases.

Role of Pulmonary Function Tests and Imaging in Diagnosis

Pulmonary Function Tests measure how much air the lungs can hold and how fast it can be breathed out, which shows whether airflow is blocked (as in asthma and COPD) and how severe it is. Imaging adds structure: chest X-rays reveal infections, fluid or masses; CT scans give detailed cross-sections for tumours or chronic damage; MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves for detailed soft-tissue images. Together, function tests plus imaging let doctors diagnose, grade and follow respiratory disease.

Pneumonia: Symptoms, Treatment and How It Differs from Other Respiratory Infections

Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue itself: its alveoli fill with fluid or pus, causing fever, cough with sputum, chest pain and breathlessness, and low blood oxygen in severe cases. Treatment depends on the cause: antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia, supportive care (rest, fluids, fever control) for viral cases, and hospital oxygen or ventilation for severe illness; the pneumonia vaccine prevents bacterial pneumonia. It differs from other respiratory infections because it affects the deep lung tissue and gas exchange, whereas bronchitis affects the airways and influenza is a more general viral illness with body aches and fatigue.

lessons.notes_html:
Nebulization Therapy: Use a nebulizer to give medication to the lungs, helping treat conditions like asthma or COPD.

Under supervision, place the prescribed medicine in the nebulizer cup, attach the mask or mouthpiece, and switch on so a fine mist is formed. The patient breathes the mist in normally until the medicine is finished, delivering the drug directly to the airways to open them and ease breathing in asthma or COPD.

Pulmonary Function Test: Measure how much air you can breathe in and out to check how well your lungs work.

Using a spirometer under supervision, breathe in fully, seal the lips around the mouthpiece, and blow out as hard and as long as possible. The readings show lung capacity and airflow, helping detect asthma or COPD and track whether treatment is working.

Assessment of Respiratory Rate: Count how many breaths a person takes in one minute to check their breathing rate.

Let the person rest and breathe normally without knowing they are being counted. Count each full breath (in and out) for one minute by watching the chest rise, and record the rate; a normal resting adult rate is about 12-20 breaths per minute, and a much faster rate suggests illness.

Use of Stethoscope to Identify Breathing Sounds: Use a stethoscope to listen to lung sounds and identify any problems like wheezing or crackling.

Place the stethoscope chest piece on the chest and back while the person breathes deeply. Normal breathing sounds are soft and even; wheezing is a high whistling sound of narrowed airways (as in asthma), and crackling is a bubbling sound of fluid or mucus in the lungs.

CO2 and Lime Water Test (Exhaled Air Experiment): Blow air into lime water and see how it changes color, showing the presence of carbon dioxide in exhaled air.

Blow gently through a straw into a test tube of clear lime water for a minute. The lime water turns milky because exhaled carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form white calcium carbonate. This proves exhaled air contains much more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.

Use of Pulse Oximeter to Measure Oxygen Saturation: Use a pulse oximeter to check how much oxygen is in a person's blood.

Clip the pulse oximeter on a fingertip, keep the hand still, and read the oxygen saturation (SpO2) and pulse rate. A normal SpO2 is about 95-100%; a lower reading, especially with breathlessness, needs prompt medical attention.

Function of Capillaries in the Circulatory System

Capillaries are the tiniest blood vessels, with walls only one cell thick. They link arteries to veins and are the place where exchange happens: oxygen and nutrients pass from blood into tissues, while carbon dioxide and wastes pass from tissues into blood.

Risk Factors for Hypertension

The risk factors are: high salt intake, obesity, lack of physical activity, smoking, excessive alcohol, chronic stress, older age, and a family history of high blood pressure. Several of these can be controlled by lifestyle change.

Coronary Artery Disease and Its Primary Cause

Coronary artery disease is the narrowing or blockage of the arteries that supply the heart muscle itself. Its primary cause is atherosclerosis: cholesterol and fatty deposits (plaque) build up on the artery walls, reducing blood flow to the heart.

ECG and What It Measures

An ECG (electrocardiogram) is a test that records the electrical activity of the heart through electrodes placed on the skin. It measures heart rate, rhythm and the timing of electrical signals, helping detect heart attacks, rhythm problems and strain on the heart.

Function of the Heart

The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: the right side pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body. Its valves keep blood flowing one way, and its steady beating supplies every tissue with oxygen and nutrients while carrying away carbon dioxide and wastes.

Hypertension: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment

Symptoms: hypertension usually has no clear symptoms, which is why it is called a silent condition, but severe cases may cause headache, dizziness or nosebleeds. Treatment: less salt, healthy weight, regular exercise, no smoking, limited alcohol, and blood-pressure medicines taken regularly, with periodic checks.

Heart Failure: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Heart failure means the heart cannot pump blood well enough for the body's needs. Causes include coronary artery disease, long-standing hypertension, heart attack damage and faulty valves. Symptoms are shortness of breath, fatigue, swollen ankles and reduced ability to exercise. Treatment is medicines to help the heart and remove excess fluid, lifestyle changes (low salt, activity as advised, no smoking), treatment of the underlying cause, and in advanced cases devices or surgery.

ECG records the heart's electrical activity and detects rhythm problems and heart attacks. An angiogram injects dye into the coronary arteries and takes X-ray pictures to detect blockages. A stress test records the heart while exercising to reveal problems hidden at rest. Echocardiography uses sound waves to show the heart's chambers, valves and pumping strength, and blood-pressure measurement plus blood tests complete the assessment. Heart Rate Measurement: Measure the number of heart beats per minute during rest and after exercise.

Find the pulse at the wrist, count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute at rest. Repeat immediately after exercise and compare: the rate rises with activity and should settle back toward resting within a few minutes in a healthy person.

Pulse Measurement: Check the pulse at different points on the body to evaluate heart rate.

Feel the pulse at the wrist (radial), neck (carotid) and, with care, other points, counting beats per minute at each. The rates should agree; a very fast, slow or irregular pulse, or a pulse that differs between points, should be reported to a teacher or doctor.

Wrap the cuff around the upper arm at heart level, inflate it, then slowly release while listening with a stethoscope (or reading the digital display). Clip the pulse oximeter on a fingertip, keep the hand still, and read blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) and pulse rate. Normal SpO2 is about 95-100%; low readings with breathlessness or chest symptoms need prompt medical attention.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Main Function of the Urinary System

The urinary system filters the blood in the kidneys, removes waste products and excess water and salts as urine, and thereby keeps the body's internal balance (homeostasis). It also helps control blood pressure and the body's water and salt levels.

Common Symptoms of a Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)

Two common symptoms are a burning feeling while passing urine and a frequent, urgent need to urinate with only small amounts passed. Other symptoms can be cloudy or bloody urine, lower abdominal pain and fever.

Most Common Cause of Kidney Stones

Kidney stones most commonly form when urine becomes concentrated with minerals, especially calcium oxalate, which crystallize instead of staying dissolved. Low fluid intake, high salt or oxalate intake and repeated urinary infections increase this risk.

Key Difference Between Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)

AKI is sudden kidney damage, often over hours or days, that is frequently reversible if the cause is treated promptly. CKD is a gradual, progressive loss of kidney function over months or years, usually from diabetes or hypertension, which is generally not reversible.

Pyelonephritis and How It Occurs

Pyelonephritis is a urinary tract infection of the kidneys. It usually occurs when bacteria, most often E. coli, travel upward from the bladder through the ureters into the kidney, causing fever, flank pain, nausea and painful urination.

Importance of Urinalysis in Detecting Urinary Infections

Urinalysis examines urine for pus cells, bacteria, blood, protein and glucose. Finding bacteria and white cells points to infection, while blood or protein can reveal kidney damage, so the test detects urinary infection and kidney disease early, cheaply and non-invasively.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
How the Urinary System Maintains Homeostasis

The kidneys filter blood and adjust what leaves in urine: they excrete excess water, salts (sodium, potassium) and wastes like urea and creatinine, while keeping needed substances. By doing this they stabilize blood volume and pressure, salt balance, acid-base balance (pH) and waste levels. When water is scarce they conserve it (concentrated urine); when there is excess they excrete it, keeping the internal environment steady despite changing intake.

Kidney Stones and Their Treatments

Kidney stones are hard deposits of minerals and salts, usually calcium oxalate, that form inside the kidney when urine is too concentrated. Small stones may pass with plenty of fluids and pain relief. Larger stones are treated by lithotripsy, which uses shock waves to break the stone into small pieces that can pass out, or by surgical removal when needed. Prevention is drinking enough water, limiting excess salt and oxalate-rich foods, and treating infections promptly.

Pyelonephritis, Cystitis and Urethritis: Transmission, Symptoms and Prevention

These are UTIs at different levels, usually caused by bacteria (most often E. coli) entering through the urethra. Urethritis is infection of the urethra, causing burning urination and discharge. Cystitis is bladder infection, causing frequent painful urination, lower abdominal pain and cloudy urine. Pyelonephritis is kidney infection, with fever, flank/back pain, nausea and vomiting in addition. Prevention for all three: drink enough water, urinate regularly and after intercourse, wipe front to back, maintain personal hygiene, and treat lower UTIs promptly before they ascend to the kidneys.

Urinalysis and the Abnormalities That Indicate Disease

Urinalysis is the laboratory examination of a urine sample: its colour, clarity, pH, and the presence of cells and chemicals. Abnormalities and their meaning: pus cells and bacteria indicate urinary infection; red blood cells indicate bleeding from the urinary tract or kidney disease; protein indicates kidney damage; glucose suggests diabetes; crystals suggest stone-forming risk; and dark or very concentrated urine can reflect dehydration. Abnormal results are confirmed with further tests.

Serum Creatinine and GFR in Diagnosing Kidney Function

Serum creatinine is a waste product from muscles that healthy kidneys excrete; when kidney function falls, its blood level rises (normal about 0.5-1.2 mg/dL in adults), so a raised value signals kidney dysfunction in both AKI and CKD. GFR (glomerular filtration rate) is calculated from creatinine, age, sex and body size and estimates how much blood the kidneys filter per minute; a falling GFR stages CKD severity and guides treatment. Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) adds information: normal 7-20 mg/dL, above 20 suggesting dysfunction or dehydration, and above 50 severe impairment.

The DRABC Approach in First Aid

DRABC stands for: D - Danger (check the scene is safe), R - Response (check whether the person responds), A - Airway (check and clear the airway), B - Breathing (look, listen and feel for normal breathing), C - Circulation (check for a pulse and signs of circulation; if absent, start chest compressions).

Signs of Cardiac Arrest

According to the chapter's table, a person in cardiac arrest may show: sudden collapse, unresponsiveness, no pulse or heartbeat, no breathing, bluish skin (cyanosis) and dilated pupils. Associated symptoms listed are chest pain, dizziness or lightheadedness, weak or irregular pulse and sudden fatigue.

Performing Chest Compressions During CPR

Place the heel of the hand on the centre of the chest, push down about 2 inches (5-6 cm) at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute, and let the chest fully recoil between pushes. For an adult, give 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths, and continue without long pauses until help arrives or the person recovers.

Primary First Aid for Burns

Cool the burn at once with cool running water for at least 10-20 minutes, remove jewellery or tight items near the burn before swelling starts, and cover it loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing. Do not pop blisters and do not apply toothpaste, butter or ice directly; for large, deep or facial burns, seek emergency medical help immediately.

The R.I.C.E Method for Sprain Management

R.I.C.E stands for: Rest - avoid using the injured area to prevent further damage; Ice - apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours to reduce swelling and pain; Compression - wrap the injured area with an elastic bandage; Elevation - raise the injured limb above heart level to reduce swelling.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
The DRABC Approach and Its Significance in Saving Lives

DRABC is the primary survey done before any treatment: Danger - assess hazards and make the area safe, approaching safely and calling for help if it is not safe; Response - talk to or tap the person gently to check responsiveness, and call for help if needed; Airway - assess, tilt the head and lift the chin, and clear obstructions; Breathing - look, listen and feel for normal breathing, since without oxygen permanent brain damage occurs within minutes; Circulation - check respiration and pulse, and if the person is unresponsive and not breathing regularly, call for help and start CPR if trained. Its significance is that it finds and fixes life threats in order, within the golden hour (the first 60 minutes after injury, most crucial for survival), instead of treating minor injuries first.

Steps and Techniques of CPR on an Adult

Steps from the chapter: ensure the scene is safe and no hazards are present; tap the person and shout to check responsiveness; call emergency services (for example Rescue 1122 in Pakistan) for help; open the airway by tilting the head and lifting the chin; check breathing; if there is no normal breathing, start chest compressions in the centre of the chest, about 2 inches deep, at 100-120 per minute, allowing full recoil; give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions; and continue CPR with minimal pauses until emergency help arrives, an AED is available, or the person starts breathing normally.

Types of Wounds and Their First Aid Management

Abrasion is a scrape from friction: clean it gently with water, remove dirt, and cover with a clean dressing. Laceration is a torn, irregular wound: apply firm pressure to stop bleeding, clean around it, and dress it; deep or gaping lacerations need medical care and possibly stitches. Puncture is a deep narrow wound from a sharp object: do not remove a deeply embedded object, control bleeding around it, and seek medical help because of infection and tetanus risk. Incision is a clean cut: apply pressure, clean, close the edges with a dressing, and seek care if it is deep, long or still bleeding.

Fractures, Sprains and Strains: Differences and First Aid Management

A fracture is a broken bone: signs are pain, swelling, deformity and inability to move the part; first aid is to immobilize the part (splint it as found), do not move the person unnecessarily, and call for help - especially for a suspected spinal fracture, where the person must be immobilized and not moved. A sprain is injury to a ligament at a joint, and a strain is injury to a muscle or tendon; both show pain, swelling and limited movement and are managed by R.I.C.E (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) and medical assessment if severe. The key difference: fractures involve bone and need immobilization and hospital care, while sprains and strains involve soft tissue and respond to R.I.C.E.

Mental and Emotional Benefits of Regular Exercise

Regular exercise reduces stress and anxiety, improves mood through endorphins, builds confidence and self-esteem, and improves sleep and concentration. It also gives a healthy outlet for emotions and a sense of achievement, which supports overall mental well-being.

Risks Associated with Overexertion During Physical Activity

Overexertion risks include muscle strain and joint injury, exhaustion and dehydration, dizziness or fainting, and in extreme cases heart attack, especially in unfit people or in heat. It also causes prolonged soreness and can force a long break from activity, undoing fitness gains.

How Exercise Contributes to Weight Management

Exercise burns calories, builds muscle that raises resting energy use, and improves metabolism and appetite control. Combined with a balanced diet, it helps prevent weight gain and supports steady, healthy fat loss without losing muscle.

Dangers of Poor Posture During Exercise

Poor posture during exercise puts uneven strain on joints and muscles, causing muscle imbalances, joint damage, back and knee pain, and a higher risk of sprains, strains and long-term injury. It also reduces the effectiveness of the exercise, since the wrong muscles do the work.

Benefits of Muscle Strength Training

Strength training increases muscle size and endurance, strengthens bones, improves posture, balance and metabolism, and makes daily tasks easier. It also protects joints, helps weight management, and reduces the risk of falls and injuries.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Physical, Mental and Emotional Benefits of Regular Exercise

Physical benefits: stronger heart and lungs, better cardiovascular health, stronger muscles and bones, improved flexibility, balance and metabolic health, and healthier weight. Mental benefits: sharper focus, better sleep and lower stress and anxiety. Emotional benefits: better mood, confidence and social connection through team activity. Together they form overall well-being: a fit body supports a calm mind, and a calm mind supports healthy habits, so the person functions better at school, work and home.

How Exercise Strengthens the Heart and Improves Cardiovascular Health

During exercise the heart must pump more blood, so it works harder and, over weeks, becomes stronger and more efficient: it pumps more blood per beat, so resting heart rate falls. Blood vessels become more flexible, blood pressure and cholesterol improve, and the body uses oxygen better. The result is improved cardiovascular health: lower risk of heart disease, hypertension and stroke, and greater stamina for daily activity.

The RICE Method in Managing Sports Injuries

RICE matters because quick, correct first aid limits swelling, pain and further damage after a sports injury, speeding recovery. Rest: stop using the injured part at once to prevent worse damage. Ice: apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours to reduce swelling and pain (never ice directly on skin). Compression: wrap with an elastic bandage, firm but not circulation-stopping, to control swelling. Elevation: raise the injured limb above heart level so fluid drains away and swelling falls. If pain, swelling or inability to move persists, seek medical care.

Consequences of Poor Posture and Improper Techniques During Exercise

Consequences are muscle imbalances, joint damage, back, knee and shoulder pain, strains and sprains, and slower progress because the wrong muscles work. lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Macronutrients and Micronutrients

Macronutrients are needed in large amounts and give energy or structure: carbohydrates (bread, rice), proteins (meat, pulses, eggs) and fats (oil, butter). Micronutrients are needed in tiny amounts but are essential for body functions: vitamins (for example vitamin A, B, C, D) and minerals (for example iron, calcium, iodine). Both groups are necessary; neither replaces the other.

Role of Proteins in the Body

Proteins build and repair tissues, including muscles, skin and organs, and they make enzymes, hormones and antibodies. They are also needed for growth in children and for healing after injury or illness.

Why Vitamins and Minerals Are Essential for Good Health

Vitamins and minerals run countless body processes: they support immunity, blood formation, bone strength, vision, nerve function and energy release from food. Even small deficiencies cause disease - for example iron deficiency causes anaemia (pale skin, fatigue), and vitamin B deficiency is worsened by alcohol abuse, which interferes with vitamin B absorption.

Balanced Diet and the Main Food Groups

A balanced diet is one that provides all nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water - in the right amounts for age, sex and activity. Its main food groups are: cereals and grains; meat, pulses and eggs (protein foods); vegetables and fruits; milk and dairy; and oils and fats in moderation, plus plenty of clean water.

Wasting and Stunting

Wasting is low weight for height, caused by recent severe undernutrition or illness, and its key sign is severe weight loss with muscle thinning. Stunting is low height for age, caused by chronic malnutrition over a long period, especially in early childhood, and it reflects long-term growth failure rather than sudden weight loss.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates, Proteins and Fats: Roles in the Body and Their Sources

Carbohydrates are the body's main energy source: sources are bread, rice, potatoes and other cereals. Proteins build and repair tissues and make enzymes and antibodies: sources are meat, fish, pulses, eggs and milk. Fats store energy, store fat-soluble vitamins, insulate the body and protect organs: sources are oil, butter, ghee, nuts and fatty fish. All three are needed in balance; excess fat in particular leads to obesity and heart disease, so oils and fats are taken in moderation.

Importance of a Balanced Diet and Dietary Guidelines

A balanced diet gives every nutrient in the right amount, supporting growth, immunity, energy and repair, and preventing both deficiency diseases and excess-weight diseases. Dietary guidelines help by translating this into daily practice: eat varied foods from all groups, favour whole grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses, limit sugar, salt and excess fat, drink clean water, and adjust portions to age and activity. Following them prevents malnutrition (undernutrition and micronutrient deficiency) and lowers the risk of chronic diseases like diabetes, heart disease and obesity.

Malnutrition: Undernutrition and Overnutrition

Malnutrition is poor nutrition from too little, too much, or an imbalanced intake of nutrients. Undernutrition is too little food or nutrients: examples are wasting, stunting and anaemia, with consequences of weak immunity, poor growth and learning, and higher death risk in children. Overnutrition is excess intake, especially of energy, sugar and fat: examples are overweight and obesity, with consequences of diabetes, heart disease, joint problems and reduced life expectancy. Both forms can exist in the same community or even household.

Stunting, Wasting and Obesity

Stunting: cause is chronic malnutrition in early childhood; symptoms are short height for age and delayed development; consequences are poor learning and lifelong reduced productivity; prevention is adequate maternal and child nutrition, breastfeeding, and clean water and sanitation. Wasting: cause is recent severe food shortage or illness; symptoms are severe weight loss and muscle thinning; consequences are weak immunity and high death risk; prevention is prompt treatment of illness, therapeutic feeding and food security. Obesity: cause is excess energy intake with low activity; symptoms are excess body fat and breathlessness on exertion; consequences are diabetes, heart disease and joint disease; prevention is balanced diet, portion control, regular exercise and less sugary drinks and junk food.

Anaemia: Causes, Symptoms, Effects and Prevention

Anaemia is a condition in which the blood has too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin, so it carries less oxygen. Causes: iron deficiency (the commonest, from low iron intake or blood loss), vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, chronic disease, and, in children and women, high iron requirements with low intake. Symptoms: pale skin, fatigue, weakness, dizziness and breathlessness. Effects: poor growth and learning in children, reduced work capacity, and in pregnancy, risk to mother and baby. Prevention: eat iron-rich foods (meat, pulses, green vegetables) with vitamin C foods to aid absorption, take iron supplements where advised (and vitamin B-rich foods or supplements if needed), treat blood loss and infections, and avoid alcohol abuse, which interferes with vitamin B absorption.

Analyse food samples to detect the presence of macronutrients (starch, proteins, and fats) using standard biochemical tests.

Starch test: add iodine solution to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch. Protein test (Biuret): add sodium hydroxide then copper sulphate; a violet colour shows protein. Fat test: rub the sample on brown paper; a translucent grease spot that remains shows fat. Record each result in a table and identify which macronutrient each food mainly provides.

Determine the pH levels of different digestive juices and explain their role in digestion.

Using pH paper or a meter under supervision, test samples standing for digestive juices: gastric juice is strongly acidic (about pH 2) so pepsin can digest protein and germs are killed; saliva is near neutral (about pH 6-7) for starch digestion in the mouth; pancreatic and intestinal juices are alkaline (about pH 8) to neutralize stomach acid so intestinal enzymes can work. Record each pH and its digestive role.

mcqs.q: In the starch test, adding iodine solution to a food sample shows starch when the colour becomes:
mcqs.why: Starch test: add iodine solution to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch. Results of each test are recorded in a table to identify each food's main macronutrient.

mcqs.q: In the protein (Biuret) test, protein is shown when, after adding sodium hydroxide and copper sulphate, the colour becomes:
mcqs.why: Protein test (Biuret): add sodium hydroxide then copper sulphate; a violet colour shows protein, while iodine giving blue-black shows starch.

mcqs.q: The fat test is done by rubbing the sample on brown paper. Fat is shown by:
options: A translucent grease spot that remains
mcqs.why: Fat test: rub the sample on brown paper; a translucent grease spot that remains shows fat. Each result is recorded in a table.

mcqs.q: Gastric juice is strongly acidic, at about pH 2, so that:
options: Pepsin can digest protein and germs are killed
mcqs.why: Gastric juice is strongly acidic (about pH 2) so pepsin can digest protein and germs are killed; saliva is near neutral (pH 6-7) and intestinal juices are alkaline (about pH 8).

mcqs.q: Saliva is near neutral, at about pH 6-7, which suits:
mcqs.why: Saliva is near neutral (about pH 6-7) for starch digestion in the mouth; gastric juice (pH 2) digests protein, and pancreatic and intestinal juices (pH 8) neutralize stomach acid.

mcqs.q: Pancreatic and intestinal juices are alkaline, at about pH 8, in order to:
options: Neutralize stomach acid so intestinal enzymes can work
mcqs.why: Pancreatic and intestinal juices are alkaline (about pH 8) to neutralize stomach acid so intestinal enzymes can work; each pH and its digestive role is recorded.

mcqs.q: In the macronutrient analysis activity, the results of the tests are:
options: Recorded in a table to identify which macronutrient each food mainly provides
mcqs.why: Students record each result in a table and identify which macronutrient each food mainly provides, using the starch, protein (Biuret) and fat tests.

mcqs.q: The iodine solution in the food tests is used to detect:
mcqs.why: Iodine solution detects starch, shown by a blue-black colour; copper sulphate with sodium hydroxide (Biuret) detects protein, and brown paper detects fat.

mcqs.q: Copper sulphate is used in which food test?
mcqs.why: Copper sulphate is added after sodium hydroxide in the Biuret protein test, giving a violet colour when protein is present.

mcqs.q: In the pH activity, the pH of digestive juices is measured using:
options: pH paper or a meter, under supervision
mcqs.why: Using pH paper or a meter under supervision, students test samples standing for digestive juices — gastric (pH 2), saliva (pH 6-7) and pancreatic/intestinal (pH 8) — and record each pH and its role.
